abstract: Quantile regression aims at modeling the conditional median and quantiles of a response variable given certain predictor variables. In this work we consider the problem of linear quantile regression in high dimensions where the number of predictor variables is much higher than the number of samples available for parameter estimation. We assume the true parameter to have some structure characterized as having a small value according to some atomic norm R(.) and consider the norm regularized quantile regression estimator. We characterize the sample complexity for consistent recovery and give non-asymptotic bounds on the estimation error. While this problem has been previously considered, our analysis reveals geometric and statistical characteristics of the problem not available in prior literature. We perform experiments on synthetic data which support the theoretical results.

summary.idea: Assume the true coefficient vector has exploitable structure, express that structure through an atomic norm, and penalize the estimator with that norm.
summary.limitations: The guarantees depend on the assumed low-complexity parameter structure. The abstract does not specify the full statistical assumptions or report tests on real datasets.
summary.problem: Quantile regression predicts a response's median or other quantiles, but estimation becomes difficult when there are more predictors than observations.
summary.results: The analysis gives sample requirements for consistent recovery and finite-sample error bounds, exposing geometric and statistical features of the problem; synthetic experiments support the theory.
summary.tldr: Structured regularization makes high-dimensional quantile estimation analyzable through explicit sample and error bounds.

title: High-Dimensional Structured Quantile Regression

abstract: Representations for semantic information about words are neces(cid:173) sary for many applications of neural networks in natural language processing. This paper describes an efficient, corpus-based method for inducing distributed semantic representations for a large num(cid:173) ber of words (50,000) from lexical coccurrence statistics by means of a large-scale linear regression. The representations are success(cid:173) fully applied to word sense disambiguation using a nearest neighbor method .

summary.idea: Learn distributed word representations from corpus co-occurrence statistics through large-scale linear regression, then compare representations with a nearest-neighbor method.
summary.limitations: The abstract does not specify the corpus, embedding dimension, disambiguation accuracy, or comparison systems, so it establishes an application rather than a quantified advantage over alternatives.
summary.problem: Language-processing systems need representations that capture word meaning across a large vocabulary.
summary.results: The method constructs representations for 50,000 words and successfully applies them to word-sense disambiguation.
summary.tldr: Corpus co-occurrence statistics can yield large-vocabulary distributed word representations useful for distinguishing word meanings.

title: Word Space
